stories.headline: Bam Adebayo says critics 'make me the scapegoat' for Heat's winless start
stories.summary: Bam Adebayo says he is being singled out as the "scapegoat" for the new-look Heat's worst start to a season in nearly two decades.
stories.body:
Bam Adebayo says he is being singled out for the new-look Miami Heat's worst start to a season in nearly two decades.

Adebayo said Monday that "outside" critics have made "me the scapegoat" after the Heat fell to 0-4 with their 113-109 loss in Miami to the Dallas Mavericks.

"Can't overthink basketball," said Adebayo, who scored just eight points on 3-of-10 shooting and missed all five of his 3-point attempts. "For me, my shot not going in. I'm not going to overthink that.

"You know, it's funny how the outside noise wants to make me the scapegoat. But when the tables turn, just all that energy -- when the energy shifts -- just be prepared for that."

Adebayo is averaging just 11.8 points and 7.3 rebounds on 40% shooting, including 16.7% from 3-point range, through his first four games this season. The Heat captain was expected to have a slight dip in production after Miami's blockbuster offseason trade for Giannis Antetokounmpo.

Adebayo also stressed that it's still very early in the season and that he is confident that the Heat will turn things around to meet their lofty standards.

"I got expectations for myself, but, obviously, the outside noise got expectations for us," he said. "So for me, I know what I'm capable of. I'm not going to overthink that. We're 0-4 right now. I'd rather it be right now than this be midway through the season or in April. Because what if we go on a 10-game winning streak? Then how does the noise change?"

When asked whether Antetokounmpo's presence is impacting his performance, Adebayo repeatedly cited his own poor long-range shooting.

"This year, I'm just taking more 3s," he said. "I mean that's that's really it. But like I said, it'll fall, and when it does ... we'll see a shift."

Heat coach Erik Spoelstra echoed Adebayo's sentiments, saying that the three-time All-Star "just needs to see the ball go in."

"He had some good, clean looks," Spoelstra said. "Just wasn't able to capitalize on them. But I know his makeup and his resiliency. We'll work together to find a way to get him aggressive in his spots where he's comfortable."

The Heat squad collectively has struggled to perform cohesively; Monday's loss marked the third time this season that Antetokounmpo was the only Miami starter with a positive true net rating for the game, according to ESPN Research.

Antetokounmpo, one of three key newcomers to Miami this season, acknowledged that the entire team is still adjusting to playing with each other.

"It's not just Bam, it's everybody," said Antetokounmpo, who recorded his first triple-double with the Heat on Monday. "You know, everybody -- we try to figure out where we fit in and what we gotta do. Kind of try to not step on our toes."

Heat guard Davion Mitchell said Adebayo needs to be "more aggressive" offensively but added that he thinks the Adebayo-Antetokounmpo partnership will eventually work.

"I think I got to do a better job of not letting [Adebayo] get lost in the game," Mitchell said. "He got to be more aggressive. I think that he will. He's still trying to figure it out because I said this before -- I think him and Giannis play in the same spaces, and then when Giannis is on the floor, he's on the floor. He can't be in those spaces, and but it's something to get used to."

The Heat, who are off to their worst start since losing their first five games of the 2007-08 season, have a road game Wednesday against the Hawks and a home game Friday against the Pacers before a five-game West Coast trip starting next Monday in Los Angeles against the Lakers.

"We have the type of guys that have the toughness to be able to handle some adversity, and collectively we'll get together and continue to forge ahead," Spoelstra said. "That's all you can do right now. Nobody cares about what's going on now with our scores. The league ... isn't going to bail us out, so it's up to us to change it."

stories.headline: A benchmark for modern F1 circuits, eyesores and aching backs: The contradictions of Austin's COTA
stories.summary: The United States Grand Prix is well-loved by fans and drivers, but there were mixed reviews coming out of the weekend.
stories.body:
Ask Lewis Hamilton, and he'll tell you Austin's Circuit of the Americas is one of the best venues in sport. Ask Carlos Sainz, and he'll tell you the circuit is the blueprint for what a modern Formula 1 racetrack should look like. Ask Max Verstappen, and he might suggest COTA's boss would struggle to walk if he did five laps of the track.

The contrasting assessments reflect the sometimes bumpy reality of running one of Formula 1's most successful events. Fourteen years after Formula 1 first arrived in the Texas capital, the United States Grand Prix is enjoying another monumental commercial success: ahead of Sunday's race, F1 confirmed a record 467,000 fans had attended across the race weekend. Remarkably, circuit boss Bobby Epstein believes the sprawling venue could have accommodated considerably more than its new record figure, and comfortably so.

While Miami and Las Vegas have brought F1's American boom to new audiences, neither's arrival has displaced Austin's reputation as a favourite among drivers and fans alike. Its appeal has always been relatively straightforward: a proper racetrack, enormous crowds and a festival atmosphere that stretches far beyond what happens on the asphalt.

But as Formula 1 has grown, so has the event around it, something which was more apparent than ever before this year. From record attendances to an enormous (and much-debated) new luxury clubhouse overlooking Turn 1, COTA is facing the same challenge confronting circuits across the calendar: how to embrace the extraordinary commercial success of modern F1 without losing the things that made it special in the first place.

"That's why we stopped selling tickets," Epstein told ESPN. "Our biggest boundary that holds us back right now are the roads that access the facility, which are scheduled to be greatly expanded within two years. And I think when that does, we should pass the half-million mark on weekend attendance.

- F1 readies Antonelli's title champagne in Austin: 'The race of a champion who isn't champion yet'

- How Kimi Antonelli can win F1 title at Mexico City GP -- with or without Qatar, Abu Dhabi races

- Max Verstappen taking painkillers to deal with 'impossible' bumps at United States Grand Prix circuit

"I think anyone going to a big event expect traffic, and they expect to wait when they come to a major world-class event like this. But I don't think anyone wants three, and four, or five-hour waits. But if we had sold 25,000 more tickets, we would have run into that. So we stopped.

"And that's our major constraint right now. It's not once they get out here. It's the last mile or so of the highway. So we stopped selling. It's both a good problem to have, and I'd much rather have it that way. I'm not complaining about that. We try to preserve the fan experience, not just while they're on property, but the experience to and from."

The fan experience was an inescapable talking point at COTA this week, with an unmissable new feature in town.

Gondolas and VIPs

Looming over the circuit's iconic first corner was an enormous new addition to the landscape, accessible via six ski-lift gondolas that go up from the paddock, over Turn 1, and back again. It features swimming pools on the roof so that invited guests can watch the racing while submerged in water, while it also boasts corporate hospitality and an almost complete view of the race track.

For some fans, it represented everything wrong with modern Formula 1: a corporate structure for big-money guests. Fans on social media pointed to the famous shot of cars as they round the final corner, with an uninterrupted view all the way up the Turn 1 hill and up to the Texas sky, where a U.S. flag would proudly wave. The new structure was unmissable on TV, as were the gondolas going back and forth, but it should be said, the Big Red grandstand on Turn 1 did not move an inch to accommodate the new building.

Seven-time world champion Hamilton, a long-time fan of Austin's venue and a big advocate of the job Epstein has done in evolving the circuit since its debut, joked that the only thing it had ruined was the previous view of the blue sky as you drove up towards Turn 1. "You just had the clouds and the flag, but you still have the flag," he said, although the flag did have to shift left to accommodate the new building.

Hamilton was unimpressed at the suggestion some fans had been critical of COTA's new feature.

"It's so easy for people to just be always negative about everything. At the end of the day it's an incredible building, the ski lift up to it is pretty phenomenal. What Bobby and his team have done with this track, if you think of the whole place, the fairground, the stage where people perform, it's an unbelievable circuit.

"I think it's one of the best overall circuits, it's super clean, access, getting in, everything. The grandstands, this whole paddock, for me it's one of the best."

McLaren's Oscar Piastri said the only impact it had on him was the first time he drove underneath the gondola, but otherwise had no issue with it.

- Kimi Antonelli wins United States GP but made to wait for first F1 title

- Fernando Alonso lashes out at 'quality of drivers' at bottom of F1 grid

"There's a bit more atmosphere, a bit more going on," Piastri said. "Before you kind of looked at the sky. Now you can see a few more people. The cable cars ... The first lap, I was like, OK, that's pretty close!

"But after that, yeah, I mean, I think it adds to the atmosphere in some ways, so it's not changed much."

It is easy to get bogged down by what a giant new corporate megastructure means for the current state of Formula 1, but it's no coincidence more and more circuits are finding ways to accommodate the growing interest from sponsors, partners and celebrities.

There's a simpler way of looking at it, too: COTA's bumper extension to 2034, the longest contract it's ever been given, was largely rooted in the building of the new facility.

"That's part of the deal," Epstein said, referring to the new Turn 1 unit. "F1 want us to build the building. Well, [we said] give us a long enough commitment so we can benefit from it."

COTA - the best circuit going, or a pain in the back?

The circuit, which debuted in 2012, has always been a favourite of drivers, thanks to its high-speed nature and the way it undulates up and down through the Texan soil. "I always say COTA is, out of all the new-generation tracks, by far the most exciting that has been designed, I think, and the most different," Sainz said ahead of the event. "And I think it's a track that a lot of circuits could take as a good example of, with the kind of design it has for overtaking, the kind of ups and downs, the roller coaster feeling. I think normally we tend to always like good old-school tracks, but Austin, even if it's not an old-school track, it feels like one. I think that's why many drivers like it and enjoy it."

The age of COTA's circuit has created a growing talking point around the event, one likely to be a recurring one as long as the circuit is on the calendar. Driver feedback on the bumpiness was mixed, but Red Bull's Verstappen came into the weekend suggesting he would need a new spine to cope with it.

He later revealed he has seen concerning X-rays showing damage to the discs in his lower back from the wear and tear of racing. In response to comments Epstein made to ESPN that everything bar Turn 1 was fine, and that Verstappen would change his mind after driving on the track again, the Dutchman fired back.

"I invite him to drive my car," Verstappen told Dutch media after qualifying second on Saturday. "I think he'd have to get out after five laps and wouldn't be able to walk anymore."

Not every driver felt the same way.

When told about other driver complaints, Hamilton said. "People are complaining, I'm 42 and my back is fine."

The Ferrari driver added: "It is bumpy, but I think it's OK ... I personally like the bumps, I think it adds character to the track, it feels flat and I love the challenge of that. The car is moving and you have to correct it, in a perfect world it would be a flat track, but then there would be lacking character. I think that's what gives this track that little bit more, it's already a great layout, but the bumps give it a bit more."

stories.headline: Kane's long road to Ballon d'Or glory ends with his crowning moment
stories.summary: After a remarkable year for Bayern Munich and England, Harry Kane becoming the world's best player is the ultimate reward for years of perseverance.
stories.body:
LONDON -- It is nine years since Harry Kane lingered at the back of the London Palladium at the end of a soccer awards show.

The Best FIFA Football Awards in 2017 had just concluded with Cristiano Ronaldo handed the men's top prize in addition to leading a team of the year including Lionel Messi, Neymar, Sergio Ramos and Gianluigi Buffon.

As the audience filed out and a few mere mortals loitered in the hope of a selfie, Kane stood near the exit, casting a longing stare at the winners on stage. He has dreamed all his life of being in their place, considered in the same breath as the game's greats.

On Monday, at the same storied West End venue, about nine miles from his birthplace in Leytonstone, he finally is. Sat next to Lamine Yamal with last year's winner Rodri one place further away, Kane kept company with the elite. And then he joined them.

Last week in Munich, he told reporters he had found the wait to learn the winner "very stressful" for himself and his family. The final few hours on Monday won't have helped. The rain present earlier in the day subsided, but the controversy did not.

Less than three hours before the ceremony was due to start, the official website published a profile of Kane as the 2026 Ballon d'Or winner. Alongside one for Kylian Mbappé and one for Yamal. They were swiftly deleted. The entire ceremony was then delayed by 45 minutes with no official reason given, amid some speculation that the notorious London traffic was responsible.

Kane won on the undercard -- the Gerd Müller Men's Award or the Striker of the Year -- to cheers from the locals in the audience. The raucous reaction from the cheap seats before addressing the crowd was a prelude to what followed. It was palpably welcome but not, by itself, an indication of the big one: Striker of the Year is not decided by vote but simply by goals, and Kane's 73 was the best in the men's game.

Having waited for over a decade to live this moment, a few extra minutes made no difference in the end.

"Wow, wow, wow," he said after taking the stage before thanking Tottenham Hotspur by saying "I wouldn't be where I am without you" in a moment of typical class.

Monday's Ballon d'Or triumph is the crowning moment for a player whose story of relentless professionalism and determined aspiration serves as an exemplar for any young player. British media is often criticized for prematurely building up players to an impossible level, only to then knock them down when that level is inevitably never reached.

Kane has always been a different case. He publicly judged himself against Ronaldo and Messi, two of the best in history, and used their devastating consistency as a target to match.

His numbers since joining Bayern Munich are staggering: 158 goals in 156 matches following a €120 million move from Tottenham in 2023. The Ballon d'Or voting period takes into account August 2025 to the end of the World Cup in July.

He scored 73 goals in 65 matches during that period, won the Bundesliga, the DFB-Pokal, the German Supercup and led England to their best FIFA World Cup finish in 60 years with third place, scoring six times at the tournament.

Back in 2017, "The Best" awards were a competition set up by FIFA as a rival to the Ballon d'Or after five years of partnership with organizers France Football had come to an end. Kane was on the 24-man shortlist for Best Men's Player that year. He finished 24th. Of course, his journey to the summit began much further back.

Coming through the Spurs academy, a young Kane had loan spells at Leyton Orient, Millwall, Norwich City and Leicester City, where you would find it extremely difficult to locate anyone honest who genuinely believed at the time they were in the presence of a future world-class talent. A nice kid, sure, a hard worker with a future in the game. But one of England's greatest?

Kane broke into Spurs' first team toward the end of the 2013-14 season and a year later was named PFA Young Player of the Year aged 21, making his England debut in the same season. He marked that moment against Lithuania with a goal then, too.

Fame was a novelty at this point. During a Tottenham preseason tour to Sydney, Kane innocently ventured out to a shopping center in his downtime. He was quickly mobbed by so many adoring fans that the club had to scramble a minibus to bring him back to the team hotel.

Kane went on to score 280 goals in 435 appearances for Spurs while breaking Wayne Rooney's all-time goal-scoring record for England. Barring injury, he will break Peter Shilton's appearance record of 125 caps next month, too.

There was, though, perhaps a sense in the buildup that Kane was not quite the global superstar his Ballon d'Or rivals were, most obviously Messi and Mbappé but also, despite his teenage years, Yamal, named Young Talent of the Year for the third consecutive year.

Former Spurs boss Jose Mourinho alluded to this in a conversation with Kane captured by Amazon in their "All or Nothing" series covering the 2019-20 campaign.

"The world looks to English football with an incredible respect but they still think that the movie stars of football belong to other places -- and I think we have to build also your status in that direction," he said.

Kane replied: "That's my aim. When you are at a club like Tottenham, of course we've done well, personally I've done well, but I want to be Ronaldo, Messi ..."

There he goes again. The Ballon d'Or is voted for by one journalist per country of FIFA's top 100 ranked nations, which brings a different dynamic than, say, the FIFA equivalent, which adds votes from national managers and captains.

He had never finished higher than 10th in the Ballon d'Or vote (2024). There are three criteria, listed in order of importance: individual performances, decisive and impressive character; collective performances and titles won; class and fair play.

And despite the Premier League being one of the United Kingdom's most successful global exports, English players have only ever won it five times (Sir Stanley Matthews, Sir Bobby Charlton and Kevin Keegan twice) and nobody has triumphed since Michael Owen in 2001.

That's more than two decades of unprecedented growth for the Premier League, and yet LaLiga often feels as though it is where the true individual talents reside. Players from Real Madrid and Barcelona have won it 12 times each. Manchester United are the most successful English club in Ballon d'Or history with four.

Kane, of course, left England in pursuit of silverware after a decade of personal achievement but collective frustration at Spurs. In doing so, he has ended up landing both silverware with Bayern and now the highest individual honor a player can attain.

"I am almost speechless," he said. "Being here in London has made it extra special. It made it a good omen for me tonight." Where once he stared at the Palladium stage, now all eyes are on him.

stories.headline: Wayne Rooney blasts Man United players amid growing crisis
stories.summary: Manchester United's players need a "firework up their a----" and reminding what it means to play for the club, according to Wayne Rooney.
stories.body:
Manchester United's players need a "firework up their a----" and reminding what it means to play for the club, according to Wayne Rooney.

Under-fire United boss Michael Carrick arrived at Carrington early on Tuesday morning with his future still up in the air. But by midday it emerged that he will remain in charge for Saturday's trip to Chelsea.

United's all-time leading goalscorer Rooney, who won five Premier League titles as well as the 2008 Champions League, feels the mentality of some the current squad must be called into question, along with the club's recruitment strategy.

"The players haven't got a leg to stand on. What's not fair is the performances they are giving," Rooney said on the Stick to United podcast on Disney+.

"I looked at the fans, you could see the pain and anger in their faces when those players are walking around the football pitch. You see [Lisandro] Martinez when [Bournemouth winger] Rayan ran round him, they are not getting to the ball, it's so frustrating.

"I could score a goal, had ability or whatever, at least I f------ ran and put myself about as a team. These players are not doing that.

"I would love to go in that dressing room and say, 'What the f--- are you all doing? What type of performances do you think this is? Do you think you deserve to wear the shirt?' Put a f------ firework up their a---- because they are not doing anything.

"We are seeing players who are numb, look like they have got no emotion, look like they don't care. Some of them might care, some good lads who are getting dragged down. It is so frustrating to watch."

Rooney feels the squad is "absolutely a million miles away" from the level needed to challenge in the Premier League again.

- Michael Carrick to lead Man United vs. Chelsea amid uncertain future - sources

- Man United are in crisis (again), but where are the Glazers?

"It is at best a mid-table team, but if you look at all the mid-table teams, what do they get? They get players working hard, running, tackling and I keep saying it, going back to the basics. These [United] players think they are better than what they are," he said.

"Unfortunately, what happened when Michael Carrick came in at the start is that it has given the players and the board false hope that they are good enough. He has done well, stuck together, managed somehow to finish third, then the board are thinking, 'We are a top four team', when in reality they are miles away from it.

"You are deluded if they think the front three are good enough. They wanted Premier League players, they have brought lads from Wolves, Brentford, who have done well, but for signings to take this Manchester United team to the next level, you are living in cuckoo land if you think they are going to achieve that."

Rooney added: "The squad is absolutely a million miles away. The worst thing for Michael Carrick, he has given the board a bit of hope when in reality, they needed a big overhaul and have done for years.

"The midfield, spending that amount on those midfielders, is absolutely crazy. I feel for Michael, he has being let down, he hasn't been good enough, but the players have let him down massively."

United lie 16th in the Premier League table in the wake of their 3-0 home defeat against Bournemouth on Sunday.

stories.headline: Nowhere to rise for Volkanovski and Yan, but Reyes and Volkov move up
stories.summary: Here's a look at every weight class to determine the best of the best in UFC, PFL and beyond.
stories.body:
Two of the greatest performances at UFC 333 earned no reward in ESPN's divisional MMA rankings.

Both featherweight champion Alexander Volkanovski, who knocked out Movsar Evloev in Saturday's main event, and men's bantamweight titlist Petr Yan, who won a trilogy fight against Merab Dvalishvili in the co-main, were already ranked No. 1 in their divisions, so there was nowhere for them to rise in those top 10s.

Evloev, who lost for the first time in his career, and Dvalishvili, an ex-champ who dropped his second straight to Yan, maintain their No. 2 rankings.

Other fights on the Abu Dhabi card did affect rankings. Light heavyweight Dominick Reyes was the lone fighter to defeat someone ranked higher than him, knocking out sixth-ranked light heavyweight Azamat Murzakanov. Reyes moves from No. 7 to the top five, and Murzakanov falls to Reyes' former spot.

Heavyweight saw a trickle-down succession of movement, partly due to a fight result. Alexander Volkov, who beat unranked Rizvan Kuniev, moves up one position to No. 3, largely because former UFC champion Tom Aspinall, previously ranked second, has been removed from the top 10 as ineligible because he has not fought in over a year. The other ranked heavyweights each move up one spot, and Kuniev enters the rankings at No. 10.

The other ranking change is at men's flyweight, where Lone'er Kavanagh climbs one position to No. 6 after handing unranked Ramazan Temirov his first loss.

Here are the ESPN pound-for-pound MMA rankings and a list of current UFC champions in all weight classes.

stories.headline: NHL Tonight: Bruins-Canes highlights another massive night of games
stories.summary: Here's what you need to know about all 11 games on the NHL calendar on Tuesday.
stories.body:
After Tuesday's games, a full four weeks of the 2026-27 NHL season will be in the books.

There have been plenty of shocks and surprises, and the schedule of games coming up promises even more.

It's not surprising that the Hurricanes are in first place in the Metro; it's quite a bit surprising that the Bruins are tops in the Atlantic. The two teams meet in Tuesday's marquee matchup (8 p.m. ET, ESPN), but there's 10 other games to monitor, too.

Here's a look at what you need to know for each game, including betting info and broadcast details:

Odds are provided by DraftKings and subject to change.

Columbus Blue Jackets at Philadelphia Flyers

7 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | CBJ -115, O/U: 5.5

Speaking of surprises, no one predicted that these two teams would be bringing up the rear in the Metro at this juncture, but here we are. (The Blue Jackets do get a little grace, as they've played just nine games so far for some reason.)

Philly has been the beneficiary of a recent heater by Matvei Michkov, who leads the team in points (eight goals, two assists). Columbus enters this game having won an overtime thriller over Vegas in its last game, with Adam Fantilli notching the game winner. Which young star shines brightest on Tuesday?

Boston Bruins at Carolina Hurricanes

8 p.m. ET (ESPN) | CAR -192, O/U: 6.5

These two franchises have had quite a history, going back to 1979-80, when the Canes were still the Hartford Whalers.

Overall, the B's hold a 115-80-24 record against Hartford/Carolina in the regular season, and a 26-16 edge in the postseason.

More recently, the Bruins won in the 2019 conference finals and the 2020 first round, while the Canes won their first-round matchup in 2022.

Both teams also have a player who ranks among the top 10 in scoring (Sebastian Aho, David Pastrnak) as well as save percentage (Pyotr Kochetkov, Jeremy Swayman).

Los Angeles Kings at Chicago Blackhawks

8 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | LA -118, O/U: 5.5

Both teams enter this matchup thankful that the Canucks exist, as Vancouver is keeping them out of the NHL's basement. But on a personal note, it's a reunion of sorts with former linemates Artemi Panarin and Patrick Kane (who played together in Chicago in 2015-16 and 2016-17, as well as in New York in the spring of 2023).

The Blackhawks got a Connor Bedard bump upon the captain's return, winning two games in a row before losing the next three. L.A. won two in a row before losing to a Devils team that was fired up about acquiring Connor Hellebuyck the day prior.

Montreal Canadiens at St. Louis Blues

8 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | STL -118, O/U: 6.5

The Canadiens continue to be without leading scorer (and captain) Nick Suzuki as he recovers from an upper-body injury. Goaltender Jacob Fowler continued his breakout campaign, backstopping the Habs to a 2-1 win in the Heritage Classic on Sunday night.

On the other side, the Blues have gone undefeated against Canadian teams so far, winning 7-2 against the Senators and 2-1 against the Jets. Will they make it 3-0?

New York Islanders at Nashville Predators

8 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | NSH -118, O/U: 5.5

The Preds have a formula for success this season: when scoring three or more goals this season, they've gone 2-0-1. The issue here is that they'll be welcoming one of the NHL's stingiest defensive teams to Bridgestone Arena. Thanks to Ilya Sorokin -- and a strong defensive structure -- the Isles have allowed just 2.55 goals per game, which is fifth fewest in the league. Which side blinks first?

New Jersey Devils at Dallas Stars

8 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | DAL -142, O/U: 5.5

It's probably too soon to expect newest Devil Connor Hellebuyck to be between the pipes for this showdown.

But for fans of elite netminding, may we interest you in some Jake Oettinger? The Stars' franchise tender has a 6-2-1 record, with a 1.43 goals-against average and .930 save percentage.

Both teams come into this matchup hot, as the Devils have won five of their past six and the Stars have won five straight.

Florida Panthers at Winnipeg Jets

8 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | FLA -130, O/U: 5.5

It's rare that a pair of interconference opponents play two games against one another so close on the calendar, but that's exactly what's happening this week for the Panthers and Jets. After this matchup Tuesday, they'll play again in Sunrise on Friday.

Given the tight proximity between matchups, might there be some message-sending or tone-setting in this one?

Minnesota Wild at Utah Mammoth

9 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | UTA -142, O/U: 6.5

There's no clearer way to set the stakes here: The winner of this game will be in first place in the Central Division after four weeks. Most expected the Wild to be one of the Central powerhouses again, but the Mammoth have arrived ahead of schedule.

On an individual basis, it's worth mentioning Kirill Kaprizov, who has 13 goals this month. That is three off of the record for goals in a single October, held by Mario Lemieux. For Utah, Clayton Keller's 15 points through 12 games put him on pace for 105 points, which would be a career high and make him the first triple-digit scorer in franchise history.

Ottawa Senators at Vegas Golden Knights

10 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | VGK -162, O/U: 6.5

Has the rest of the NHL figured out the Golden Knights? Vegas enters Tuesday's action on a three-game losing streak, though they remain in second place in the Pacific Division thanks to an 8-2-0 start. The Sens have been on opposite sides of lopsided affairs the past three games: a 5-1 win over the Panthers, then a 6-2 loss to the Sharks, then a 7-4 win over the Rangers.

Which team's superstar will reign supreme Tuesday? Ottawa's Tim Stutzle has 16 points through 12 games, while Vegas' Jack Eichel has 19 through 13.

Vancouver Canucks at Anaheim Ducks

10 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | ANA -198, O/U: 6.5

stories.headline: Bafana boss Pitso Mosimane's latest South Africa squad shows favouritism fears were unfounded
stories.summary: Mosimane has made several changes from his first preliminary squad, which he announced almost immediately after taking charge at the beginning of September.
stories.body:
When Pitso Mosimane returned as Bafana Bafana head coach, sceptics feared that his proximity to South African club football would lead to an erosion of the meritocratic culture Hugo Broos had built, but the 62-year-old's second preliminary squad suggests it has only been enhanced.

Mosimane began his tenure with Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON) qualifying wins over Guinea and Eritrea and a friendly victory over Egypt. Next up is the AFCON qualifying double-header against Kenya on Nov. 13 & 17.

Mosimane has made several changes from his first preliminary squad, which he announced almost immediately after taking charge at the beginning of September.

Chicago Fire's Mbekezeli Mbokazi has returned from injury, while Aden McCarthy, Botiumelo Radiopane, Nqaba Xulu, Luke le Roux, Thalente Mbatha, Nkosikhona Radebe, Devin Titus and Thakasani Mbanjwa have also received call-ups.

For every one of these call-ups, a layman can deduce a clear possible motive. McCarthy is the most obvious among them -- he has consistently featured at centre-back for Sabah in the UEFA Champions League and performed well at the highest level.

Radiopane and Xulu are in hot scoring form domestically for Orlando Pirates and Richards Bay respectively. Titus has earned his place with a strong start to life at MAS Fes in Morocco. Mbatha is back from injury and le Roux on the books of a new club at Cercle Brugge after struggling for game time at Portsmouth.

Radebe adds a right-back option from an in-form AmaZulu side with Mamelodi Sundowns' Khuliso Mudau still on the mend from injury. Mbanjwa is rewarded for a strong start to the season in goal for Golden Arrows.

Yanela Mbuthuma and Shandre Campbell -- both of whom have experienced dips in form and fortune at club level since the last international break -- are notable absentees.

In cutting two players he had given opportunities to after they had been mostly overlooked by Broos, Mosimane suggested he is willing to operate without fear or favour.

When 'Jingles' was on the verge of being appointed, Broos was quoted as telling Het Nieuwsblad: "You know, South Africa still don't have a coach. The candidate is Pitso Mosimane, a successful South African coach.

"But they know that if he comes in, they'll go five years back in time. Club owners and agents calling coaches to influence the squad selection. I threw all of them out. If one called, I would say bluntly: 'I don't talk with agents'."

The concern over agents and owners trying their luck in influencing the Bafana head coach may have been well-founded. Broos was not the first to complain of this within the national team setup.

However, questioning if Mosimane himself was open to influence without proof he was willing to make publicly available was ill-advised. It is impossible to accurately speculate on what conversations have or have not gone on between Mosimane and club owners and agents in the two months since then, but what is clear is that his team selection has been thoroughly meritocratic.

The momentum he has garnered is reminiscent of what Broos achieved in the first six months of his tenure.

At the time, the Belgian's irreverent team selection and approach to squad culture put everybody on their toes and led to an uptick in results. After they had failed to qualify for AFCON 2021 immediately before Broos was appointed, the Belgian fell narrowly short of steering Bafana into qualification playoffs for the 2022 World Cup.

In subsequent years, he kicked on and led Bafana to third place at AFCON 2023 (held belatedly in Ivory Coast in early 2024) and the 2026 World Cup round of 32.

When discussing the most successful Bafana Bafana coaches of all-time, Broos should be placed alongside Clive Barker in the top two. However, even the brightest tacticians eventually settle on patterns in their squad selection, and towards the end of his tenure, the Belgian became more predictable in certain aspects.

There was a fairly settled back five of Ronwen Williams, Aubrey Modiba, Mbokazi, Ime Okon and Mudau, and until he switched up his attacking plan to revive the FIFA World Cup campaign, Broos was likely to start Lyle Foster upfront with Evidence Makgopa the main alternative.

In midfield, Teboho Mokoena was a near certain starter and Sphephelo Sithole the clear preferred option alongside him, although Broos occasionally tinkered with his formation and left room for the likes of Bathusi Aubaas and the late Jayden Adams in the holding role. Nkosinathi Sibisi was considered another option, occasionally stepping out from the back into midfield.

Mosimane's arrival has reopened competition for places in these positions. Brooklyn Poggenpoel is retained in the squad after impressing in midfield over the last international break.

After Mbuthuma's minutes upfront, Radiopane and Xulu have been given a chance to earn theirs. Foster has made a second successive preliminary squad, although he failed to make the final squad last time out while in the process of leaving Burnley on loan to Houston Dynamo and settling in.

Fawaaz Basadien, Olwethu Makhanya, and McCarthy are in consideration in the backline. Mudau is, however, still the likely first-choice at right-back for the time being when he returns to full fitness. Still, Mosimane has done well to identify alternatives.

Mosimane declined to get drawn into a war of words with Broos over anything not directly related to matters on the pitch and instead praised his predecessor's impressive record as Bafana head coach.

In his first stint, Mosimane may not have succeeded in the hotseat. However, early results and his approach to team selection suggest he has justified the decision of the South African Football Association (SAFA) to give him a second chance and trust him to navigate the role without fear or favour to anyone.

stories.headline: Who I would -- and would not -- want to be this AFL offseason
stories.summary: The AFL offseason is in full swing but it won't stop us from analysing the landscape. Here's who Jake Michaels would (and wouldn't!) want to be heading into 2027.
stories.body:
From Brisbane's stunning three-peat to Fremantle's Grand Final capitulation, high-profile free agent signings to ongoing legal battles, so much has happened in the AFL world over the past month. So, who would you want to be (and not want to be) this off-season.

All of our best footy content, now on Instagram. Follow @espnfooty here!

Those I WOULD NOT want to be this AFL offseason
Ross Lyon
No coach will enter season 2027 under more scrutiny and pressure than Ross Lyon. St Kilda was widely tipped to rise up the ladder this season just gone after being the most active club during the previous trade and free agency period. Instead, the Saints severely underwhelmed, winning just 10 games and finishing a disappointing 11th on the ladder, 10 premiership points outside of the wildcard finals. The club is desperate to retain the services of superstar midfielder Nasiah Wanganeen-Milera, who is out of contract at season's end and could easily be tempted with a blockbuster move back to South Australia. As a result, St Kilda's powerbrokers likely won't tolerate another sluggish start, which means Lyon has absolutely zero margin for error in 2027.

Fremantle fans
Alright, alright, I'm sorry to bring it up again. And please feel free to skip ahead if you don't want to re-live it once more. But the reality is every single Dockers fan will be replaying those harrowing final four-and-a-bit minutes of the Grand Final in their mind all offseason, wondering how on earth their team coughed up what appeared to be an insurmountable late lead. The heartbreaking loss to Brisbane is as devastating as it gets for a footy club and you could almost understand if any Fremantle fan never wanted to watch the sport again. Seriously, I'm not sure how you ever get over that loss. It all just means the next five months are going to feel like an eternity.

Andrew McGrath
It was an incredibly disappointing season from new Essendon skipper Andrew McGrath, who averaged a career-low in disposals, kicked just two goals, and failed to poll a single Brownlow Medal vote. To be a captain of a club that won just two games for the entire year and still be unable to crack the top 10 of the best and fairest count is pretty embarrassing, really. With former skipper Zach Merrett now no longer at the club, McGrath, who has now been in the league for a decade and tallied 200 games, is Essendon's main man. It's time he starts to play like it or else he risks further damage to his reputation.

Chris Fagan's replacement
Whoever is entrusted with the task of succeeding Chris Fagan at the Lions will be feeling the pressure and the eyes of the footy world on them from day one. It's a bit like following Jerry Seinfeld on stage. How can you possibly back up that act!? Fagan completely revitalised Brisbane, leading the club out of the doldrums and to its second three-peat this century. And while Fagan's tenure is up and dual Brownlow medallist Lachie Neale has departed for Collingwood, nobody feels as if the Lions are over the hump. In fact, quite the contrary. The age profile of this list should have them contending for years to come. That can be both a blessing or a curse for any new coach.

The Pullman Five

Okay, this one might be a tad on the nose, but who would want to be one of Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, Nick Blakey, Riley Bice, or James Jordan this offseason? The incident at the Pullman Hotel in Melbourne on the eve of finals remains a legal matter, meaning there are still so many unknowns when it comes to the footballing careers of these five. Can Heeney and Warner ever ingratiate themselves to the Swans' faithful once more? Will Bice and Jordan be shuffled out of the best team? And then there's Blakey. North Melbourne gave up the farm for his signature and much will be expected of him at his new club. I'm just not sure he's the difference maker they think he is.

An (existing and competing) expansion club
At what point do we stop referring to Gold Coast and GWS as expansion clubs? Probably now. But I'm lumping them together in here for different reasons. The Suns were a total shambles this year, falling from flag favourite after three rounds to finishing in the bottom six and winning just two games after the mid-season byes. Spearhead Ben King has now departed the club and rumour has it Matt Rowell wants to follow suit. Damien Hardwick is under the pump and must show something in year four at the helm. Meanwhile, the Giants just held a fire sale, clearing out Toby Greene, Jesse Hogan, Lachie Whitfield, and Kieren Briggs. It's a bold move, and while it could pay dividends down the track, you figure there simply has to be some short term pain.

Those I WOULD want to be this AFL offseason
Zach Merrett
This time last year Merrett would have been top of my other list, but the veteran midfielder's wish of a fresh start at a new club has now been granted, and that must feel like an enormous weight has been lifted from his shoulders. Merrett joins the Hawks, a club which could easily have won the premiership this year if not for Hugh McCluggage's late heroics during preliminary final weekend. It means that for the first time in Merrett's career he will enter a season truly believing his side can go all the way. That's got to be a great feeling for an elite player who has toiled away for so long and enjoyed little success.

Nasiah Wanganeen-Milera
As we've established, his coach might be under immense pressure, but Wanganeen-Milera certainly shouldn't be feeling the pinch. In fact, he goes into next season with all options and possibilities on the table. If the Saints turn out to make good on their promise from last year and actually show they can compete with those at the pointy end, then he may well elect to sign on and remain at the club. But if 2027 turns out to be more of the same, he will have his choice of 17 new destinations to call home, including the two clubs from his home state of South Australia. Make no mistake, Wanganeen-Milera will be both the most discussed and in-demand player in the sport next season.

Andrew Mackie and Geelong's entire recruitment staff
When the siren sounded on the trade and free agency period, Geelong list boss Andrew Mackie should have been pumping his fists and popping bottles of champagne in celebration. The Cats have been arguably the biggest winners of the offseason to date, improving across every line with additions of former Giants captain Toby Greene, reliable ruck Rowan Marshall, and still criminally underrated key defender Jordan Ridley. It's a hefty haul and a great salvage after the club discovered at the eleventh hour it would be missing out on the services of Zak Butters. Mackie and his team have done their job, now it's over to Chris Scott and the playing group.

Fremantle fans
Alright, so there are the obvious reasons why you wouldn't want to be a Fremantle fan this offseason, but there are also plenty of reasons why you absolutely would. The Dockers came within an inch of winning their first premiership last month and proved to the footy world, and their supporters, the club has a list to not only go all the way in 2027 but remain one of the premier sides in the league for the next half decade. Just about everyone on this Fremantle squad is yet to hit their prime and has serious scope to improve next year. That should be both a worrying thought for the other 17 clubs and a great comfort to those who cheer for the men in purple.

Jason Horne-Francis
The departure of superstar midfielder Zak Butters during free agency means the keys to Port Adelaide now firmly belong to Horne-Francis. Some might argue he's shared those keys with Butters in recent years, but there's simply no denying who will be top dog at Port heading into next season. Horne-Francis is still just 23 years of age but he has shown he possesses all of the attributes to succeed as his club's main man. I expect him to relish the extra responsibility, too, and take his game to even greater heights. Jason, train hard and we'll see you in 2027!

Jaymie Graham
It must feel pretty special knowing a club made the decision to part ways with a four-time premiership-winning coach in favour of you, despite the fact you've never coached a senior AFL game. Graham arrives at Arden Street with an impressive resume as an assistant and has been tasked with ending North Melbourne's decade-long finals drought. Some will make the case he faces similar pressure to whoever takes over from Fagan at the Lions, but I see his role, at least in the immediate future, as one which carries far less of a burden. Given North's recent struggles, he will be offered (a little) time to get things right. His team is also in the sweet spot of being enough to win with now but not good enough to carry crazy expectation.

stories.headline: NRL transfer whispers: Cochrane set for Ipswich Jets; Samrani to test open market
stories.summary: The NRL season may be over, but the player market is already heating up ahead of November 1. Isaac Issa has news from the Dragons on some key outside backs
stories.body:
The NRL season may be over, but the player market is already heating up ahead of November 1, with clubs beginning to shape their rosters for 2027 and beyond.

From player movement to changes behind the scenes, ESPN NRL Insider Isaac Issa has the latest whispers from around the competition.

Samrani expected to test open market
Jordan Samrani is expected to test the open market from November 1. ESPN understands he will explore his options for 2028 and beyond.

Following a breakout season with the Parramatta Eels, Samrani is open to assessing opportunities elsewhere when the contracting window opens on Sunday.

Cochrane set to link up with Titans feeder

Taye Cochrane is set to link up with Gold Coast Titans feeder club Ipswich Jets for the 2027 season following his departure from Canterbury.

ESPN understands the young fullback has signed with the Queensland Cup outfit after the Bulldogs opted against offering him a contract for next season.

Cochrane scored six tries in 14 NSW Cup appearances for Canterbury in 2026, having been part of the club's Jersey Flegg premiership-winning side in 2024.

The move follows Phil Gould's confirmation that Cochrane would leave the Bulldogs, with ESPN revealing he had not been offered a new deal.

Bulldogs opt against Cochrane deal

Canterbury have opted against offering Taye Cochrane a contract for 2027, with the young fullback set to depart Belmore.

ESPN understands Cochrane was not offered a new deal, following Phil Gould's confirmation he would not remain at the Bulldogs next season.

Cochrane scored six tries in 14 NSW Cup appearances this year, playing predominantly at fullback.

He was part of Canterbury's 2024 Jersey Flegg premiership-winning side before progressing to NSW Cup the following season.

Panthers make retention intentions clear on Patea
Penrith have informed Luron Patea's management of their desire to retain the young prop beyond 2027, although he still intends to test the open market from November 1.

ESPN understands multiple clubs are interested in speaking to Patea, who is approaching the final year of his Panthers contract.

ESPN previously reported that Penrith had yet to begin extension discussions with Patea.

Tigers keen to retain Mason

Wests Tigers are keen to retain Heath Mason, with the club working through roster space to accommodate the young utility.

ESPN understands Mason remains part of the Tigers' long-term plans, although his future is yet to be resolved ahead of 2027.

Cowboys open to keeping Taumalolo

North Queensland are open to retaining Jason Taumalolo beyond 2027, with the veteran forward's assessment of how his body is holding up set to guide the next step.

ESPN understands the Cowboys will take their lead from Taumalolo as he weighs up his playing future, reflecting his standing as a club legend.

Taumalolo is contracted until the end of next season and becomes eligible to negotiate with rival clubs for 2028 onwards from November 1.

Panthers lock in Patea
Penrith have secured Tua Patea until the end of 2029, with the youngster signing an extension that includes a pathway from a development contract into the club's top 30.

Patea capped off the 2026 season with a hat-trick in the Panthers' Jersey Flegg Grand Final victory, having started the year with an NRL training block.

The new deal will see him join Penrith's full-time NRL squad as he works towards a first-grade debut.

Bulldogs closing in on Skelton return

Jeral Skelton is closing in on a return to Canterbury following his departure from the Wests Tigers.

ESPN understands the Bulldogs are in advanced discussions to bring the outside back to the club for the 2027 season.

An agreement is understood to be close, although the deal has yet to be finalised.

Multiple NRL sides eye Knights forward

A Sydney club and a Queensland-based club are monitoring Newcastle forward Mat Croker ahead of November 1.

ESPN understands the two clubs have shown interest in the 27-year-old, who is approaching the final year of his Knights contract and can negotiate with rivals for 2028 onwards from next month.

Rivals keeping tabs on Dragons' Tu

Multiple clubs are monitoring St George Illawarra outside back Setu Tu, with the Dragons yet to begin talks over a contract extension.

Tu is contracted until the end of 2027 and is expected to test the open market from November 1, when rival clubs can negotiate a deal for 2028 and beyond.

The former Warriors outside back joined the Dragons on a development contract this season and is set to move into the club's top 30 squad in 2027.

His ability to cover multiple positions across the backline adds to his appeal as clubs assess their recruitment options.

Roosters eye Dockar-Clay reunion
The Roosters have shown interest in a potential return for Zach Dockar-Clay as they explore options to bolster their hooking and utility depth.

ESPN understands the 31-year-old has emerged as an option following his departure from Manly, with discussions remaining at an early stage.

Dockar-Clay spent the 2024 and 2025 seasons with the Roosters before joining the Sea Eagles on a one-year deal for 2026.

Manly confirmed his departure last month after a season in which he claimed the club's NSW Cup best-and-fairest award.

Bostock brushes Dragons links

Dolphins star Jack Bostock has dismissed recent links between himself and the Dragons, admitting this isn't the first time he'd been floated for a club switch.

"I've been linked to a few a clubs," Bostock admitted.

"I don't know about [the Dragons links]."

He said that while he "obviously sees it in the media," his sole focus is the Kangaroos.

Sloan's Dragons stay still a possibility

Tyrell Sloan could yet remain at St George Illawarra next season, with discussions ongoing over a potential stay despite his planned move to Castleford.

There is interest in keeping Sloan at the Dragons, but several hurdles remain before that can become a reality.

Roster space and salary cap room would need to be worked through, while any arrangement would also require Castleford to agree to release him.

Sloan previously admitted he would "love to" remain in the NRL when speaking to Channel Nine in August, after his Castleford deal had been announced.

No agreement has been reached and a stay is far from guaranteed.

stories.headline: Inside the stunning 72-hour Lakers sale -- and the uncertainty that still looms
stories.summary: Three days of secret talks resulted in Mark Walter flipping the Lakers -- and reignited yet another round of bickering among the six Buss siblings.
stories.body:
BOB IGER WAS on his 213-foot sailing superyacht on Aug. 12, winding down a monthlong vacation in Europe following a historic, two-decade run as CEO of Disney.

The biggest event of the day was supposed to be the first total solar eclipse over the continent in more than a century.

Millions of tourists, including Iger, had booked vacations along the eclipse's path from Greenland to Southern Spain during the syzygy -- a word derived from Ancient Greek for "yoked together" -- which describes a rare astronomical event in which three or more celestial bodies align in a straight line.

During a solar eclipse, the moon sits exactly between the sun and Earth, casting its shadow onto Earth. Some enjoy the rare view -- through special sunglasses.

Others ascribe great meaning and magic to eclipses. As those tourists headed to viewing spots for the solar eclipse across Europe, Iger was in a wholly different syzygy with his longtime friend and business partner Josh Kushner and Los Angeles Lakers owner Mark Walter.

The alignment of three financial heavy hitters was about to turn what should have been a once-in-a-generation event -- last year's record-breaking sale of the Lakers from the Buss family to Walter -- into the NBA's most shocking news -- again.

Instead of getting into position to watch the solar eclipse, Iger was furiously working the phones from Italy to consummate a stunning event of his own -- a $12.5 billion sale of the Lakers seemingly out of nowhere, creating an eclipse unto itself across the worlds of sports and business.

Little did anyone know that these secret, cross-continental talks were about to put the Lakers in significant transition yet again -- with new owners evaluating everything and everyone; squabbling former owners again jostling for power and money; and an overhauled roster finally built in the image of its superstar, Luka Doncic.

Interviews with more than a dozen team insiders, league executives and others with intimate knowledge of the sale reveal how the deal, which was made over a furious 72 hours, upstaged an already-transformative offseason -- and reignited yet another unresolved round of messy public bickering among the six Buss siblings that still hangs uncomfortably over the beginning of this new season.

JUST A YEAR ago, Lakers governor Jeanie Buss had shocked the sports world by negotiating a sale to Walter after 46 years of family ownership. Though that deal was eventually approved by all six siblings, it was not a clean process.

According to several family sources, younger brothers Joey and Jesse Buss -- who, because of a "last-man standing" provision in Dr. Jerry Buss's family trust, were positioned to run the team one day after their older siblings died -- hadn't responded to the vote when the sale was initially announced.

If the family was going to sell, Joey and Jesse wanted to be a part of the process. They had recently pitched to the other siblings a way to sell a minority share -- albeit, sources with knowledge of the discussions said, at a lower valuation than the $10 billion their older sister subsequently agreed to in the deal with Walter. The younger Buss brothers eventually joined their four older siblings in voting for the sale to Walter, but the process created animosity.

Several siblings grumbled that Jeanie had not opened the bidding to outside buyers and had, instead, negotiated directly with Walter, multiple family sources said.

Walter, who already owned 27% of the Lakers, had the right of first refusal on any eventual sale of the Buss family's remaining shares, but how did anyone know how much the team would've fetched without actually putting it on the open market?

The relationship between Jeanie and her siblings disintegrated further when the Lakers, with Jeanie's approval, fired Janie, Joey and Jesse from their respective positions with the franchise within two months of closing on the sale.

All three had expected they'd keep their roles for at least some time while Jeanie was still the controlling owner, multiple family sources said.

The deal with Walter included contractual language to keep Jeanie in charge for the next five seasons but contained no such protections for any other family members.

Janie told ESPN's Baxter Holmes last season that her sister's actions had made her feel disrespected, like a "crumpled-up piece of paper thrown into the trash." She cited the desires of their father, who had purchased the Lakers in 1979 and died in 2013.

"I don't think my dad would be happy with the way things just went down," Janie told Holmes. "Not at all."

There was even more consternation, those sources said, when the Buss family members were suddenly charged more for hospitality and their tickets to Lakers games shortly before the start of the playoffs as part of a larger restructuring of Lakers business practices.

That familial tension simmered throughout last season -- and came to a boil once again this summer.

FOR MUCH OF 2026, Iger and Kushner had been leading a group bidding for the potential Las Vegas NBA expansion franchise, which the NBA initially projected to go for $6 billion-$8 billion, according to industry and ownership sources.

But those bids had blown by that threshold, those sources said, and were approaching the then-record $10 billion valuation of Walter's sale.

Whichever group won the expansion bid would likely then need to spend what multiple sources estimated would be an additional $2 billion -- at least -- to build an arena in Las Vegas.

The Kushner-Iger group had been regarded as one of the favorites to land the team. Iger has had a longtime business relationship with NBA commissioner Adam Silver, from Iger's days negotiating broadcast rights deals for ABC/ESPN with the NBA. In 2020, the two collaborated with the NBPA to create "the bubble" at the Walt Disney Resorts in Orlando, Florida, where the NBA finished its season amid the COVID-19 pandemic. Iger had also been a longtime season-ticket holder of the LA Clippers, although he notably canceled them last season over the team's treatment of Chris Paul, a close friend of Iger's, sources close to him said.

Other finalists for the Las Vegas expansion franchise included groups headed by Walmart heiress Nancy Walton Laurie and her husband Bill Laurie; Las Vegas Golden Knights owner Bill Foley and former Phoenix Suns CEO Jerry Colangelo; and Canadian businessman Steve Apostolopoulos and former Milwaukee Bucks owner Marc Lasry.

As the Aug. 10 deadline for bids approached, Kushner and Iger discussed their options.

Over the past two decades, the 41-year-old Kushner had made a fortune building his venture capital fund, Thrive Capital, with investments in technology companies such as Instagram, Spotify, Twitch, Stripe and OpenAI. This year, Kushner started a new fund, Thrive Eternal, as a hedge against artificial intelligence.

"These are assets with qualities that cannot be replicated by technology," Thrive Eternal says on its website. "Iconic franchises and cultural institutions rooted in tradition, identity, and shared experience. In a world shaped by abundant intelligence where creation scales and distribution fragments, we believe they will matter even more."

An expansion team is not exactly an iconic brand or a legacy franchise. The Lakers, New York Knicks, Chicago Bulls and Boston Celtics are. None of those was known to be for sale, however. The Knicks had just won an NBA title. The Celtics and Lakers had recently been sold to new owners for record amounts. The Bulls were firmly in the hands of the Reinsdorf family, who have not shown any interest in selling.

Still, Kushner and Iger kicked around the idea.

Would any of the owners of those franchises take a phone call or listen to an offer? How much would it take to pique their interest?

It was a bold, risky pivot to even make calls while they were in the throes of the expansion process. If word got out that they were considering moving away from the expansion franchise, would it risk their standing with the NBA?

Whatever they did would need to be quick -- and quiet.

WALTER WAS ON a ranch with spotty cellphone service on Aug. 9, when he got a call from a friend, asking whether he'd consider selling the Lakers, according to three sources with knowledge of his whereabouts and thinking.

The first conversation was short. The Lakers weren't for sale, Walter told his friend, who relayed the message to Kushner and Iger. But the two businessmen had reason to persevere in their efforts.

Two days earlier, on Aug. 7, they had called a well-connected financial industry source who was close enough to Walter to suggest he might be looking to restructure some of his business assets amid federal investigations of alleged fraud within his sprawling $365 billion financial empire, according to multiple sources with knowledge of the conversations.

They figured it was worth dropping a line in the water, baiting the hook at a number that would make him think about it.

The only catch was they needed an answer within 24 hours. There was no time for a long negotiation or intermediaries.

Kushner made the next call to Walter, according to multiple sources with knowledge of the negotiation, and Kushner offered to buy Walter's shares at a $12.5 billion valuation -- a 25% increase in 14 months.

It was the kind of staggering "Godfather offer" Walter had presented to Jeanie Buss when he convinced her to sell him the majority of her family's shares a year earlier.

Walter decided to cut short his weekend trip and get to a place with better cellphone reception. They had his attention. By Monday, he had returned to his estate in White Oak, Florida.

He called his wife, Kimbra, and daughter, Samantha, and asked what they thought of him selling the Lakers.

He outlined the enormous return he'd make at this valuation -- nearly $4 billion because he had bought the first 27% of his Lakers shares at a $5 billion valuation in 2021 -- and the benefits that liquidity could provide him, given the remediation plans he had proposed to state insurance regulators.

Neither his wife nor daughter had an issue with him selling the Lakers, those sources said. They had been involved with the Los Angeles Dodgers for 14 years, but their attachment to the Lakers was still new.

After Walter's family signed off, the circle of people involved in the negotiations widened.

Advisers on both sides were sworn to secrecy. There wasn't time for Kushner and Iger's group to do anything resembling due diligence. They were buying the brand, as is, with as quick a close as you'll ever see in a $12.5 billion deal.

By the evening of Aug. 11 -- 72 hours after the idea had first been presented to him -- Walter had come to an agreement with Iger and Kushner.

JEANIE BUSS LEARNED of Walter's agreement to sell his shares of the Lakers hours before ESPN reported the news on the morning of Aug. 12, according to multiple sources with knowledge of their conversations.

She was stunned, according to sources close to her.

This was not what she had planned for or expected when she reached out to Walter in 2021 to suggest he purchase Philip Anschutz's shares to become the largest minority shareholder in the franchise, and with it, hold the first right of refusal to buy the Buss family's shares for a controlling interest in the team.

Walter and Buss had built a relationship over many years before he expressed an interest in buying into the Lakers.

Over the decade he owned the Dodgers, Walter had actively built bridges between L.A.'s premier baseball team and its basketball team. Lakers legend Magic Johnson was part of Walter's ownership group. Dodgers players were often invited to and hosted at Lakers games, and vice versa. Walter often attended games with Buss, while Buss attended Dodgers games with Walter.

At the time he bought Anschutz's shares, only people very close to the situation understood why it was so significant. Buss had essentially chosen Walter as her successor. Whenever she was ready to sell her family's controlling shares, he would have the inside track to buy them.

Buss chose Walter, multiple sources close to her said, because of how he owned and operated the Dodgers and the positive reviews he had gotten from associates of hers, including Johnson, tennis legend Billie Jean King and longtime Dodgers executive Lon Rosen. She had compared him to her father, Dr. Jerry Buss, for his commitment to winning publicly and privately over the years.

To those close to the situation, the question wasn't whether the Buss family would eventually sell to Walter but when. Older brothers Johnny and Jim had wanted to sell the team for years.

Jeanie, her sister Janie and younger brothers Joey and Jesse still had roles with the team and wanted to stay on longer.

In 2025, Walter came up with an offer he thought would make everyone happy: a $10 billion valuation -- generating approximately $800 million for each sibling -- and an agreement for Jeanie to stay on as controlling owner for five years, codified in writing as part of the agreement.

"Over the past decade, I have come to know Mark well -- first as a businessman, then as a friend and now as a colleague," Jeanie Buss said in a statement after the sale. "He has demonstrated time and time again his commitment to bringing championships to Los Angeles, and, on behalf of Lakers fans everywhere, I am beyond excited about what our future has in store."

Buss even showed that paperwork to Doncic and his team, his manager Lara Beth Seager said, to reassure them that she would still have final say over his basketball future.

Doncic had learned the hard way how an ownership change could affect him after his shocking trade from the Dallas Mavericks to the Lakers in February 2025.

Former Mavericks owner Mark Cuban also thought he'd be allowed to stay on as head of basketball operations when he sold his controlling stake to the Adelson family in 2023. Cuban swore to Doncic that he wanted him to be a Maverick for life, but wasn't involved or included in the trade discussions that sent Doncic to L.A.

This time, it was Jeanie who would learn the hard way -- that whatever relationship she had built with Walter and others would be superseded by the harsh realities of the modern business world.

DESPITE THAT RELATIONSHIP, the man Jeanie chose as the next steward of the Lakers was not the rock-solid titan of the financial industry he appeared to be.

Walter, the public would soon learn, was under multiple federal criminal investigations before his purchase of the Lakers became official at the end of October. According to the Wall Street Journal, the FBI on Sept. 18, 2025, conducted a raid of a private plane at Chicago's Midway Airport, where Walter had been traveling, and seized a laptop and mobile phone.

Just 10 months later, Walter flipped the Lakers like a cold asset, not a crown-jewel, generational investment.

After five decades of family ownership, Jeanie had relinquished control of her family's most prized possession to someone who had treated it no differently than any other line item in his massive portfolio.

"I mean, he made $2.5 billion in 10 months by flipping the Lakers like a spec house," one family confidant said. "But that wasn't supposed to be the deal. Jeanie picked him because he was going to own it like he's owned the Dodgers."

Walter has not spoken publicly about the sale outside of an initial statement he released to ESPN.

In late August, his company, The Walter Group, issued a statement asserting it had been subjected to "multipronged attacks" from "unnamed sources with self-serving interests."

The statement said that TWG and its Group 1001 insurance companies had presented a plan to state insurance regulators to address regulatory concerns over a percentage of affiliated transactions it had misreported in its filings. TWG explained that the affiliated transactions in question are "common across the insurance industry" and "suggestions that TWG is looting insurers is defamatory and false."

Investigators are still looking into the company's dealings as it makes changes in the way it operates. TWG Global announced in late August that it had swapped out $6.5 billion of its assets to replace the type of affiliated loans regulators had taken issue with. The dual sales of the Lakers and Walter's minority 12.8% stake in Premier League club Chelsea have raised additional capital, while also leading to an assortment of buyers inquiring about the availability of the Dodgers and Los Angeles Sparks.

The company has emphatically denied that it is looking to sell its sports assets at "fire sale" prices to raise capital for its insurance operations. The sales of the Lakers and Chelsea came in at significant valuations -- a record in the case of the Lakers. However, sources with knowledge of the situation confirm a Bloomberg report that acknowledged there have been early-stage discussions about the Sparks at what would be a similarly massive valuation, estimated at $700 million.

Inquiries for the Dodgers have thus far been rebuffed, those sources said.

IGER LANDED BACK home in Los Angeles a few days after the sale agreement was reached. The first visitor he entertained at his house was Jeanie Buss, according to multiple sources with knowledge of the meeting.

He had given public comments to the California Post immediately after news of the sale broke that the new ownership group intended to honor the agreement Buss had with Walter to stay on as controlling owner, but added, "if something changes, then it changes."

Despite the public hedge, Iger reaffirmed his commitment to Jeanie to maintain a role after the sale closes when they met, those sources said. They have stayed in regular contact since then.

Whether she'll be able to do so -- and what that role ultimately is -- depends on how the latest round of family discord is resolved.

By the time Walter decided to sell his stake in the Lakers in mid-August, family sources said there had already been renewed calls among the siblings to sell the remaining 17.8% of the team that the family owned.

The Lakers had fired four of her siblings already. Jim Buss, who was fired in 2017, noted to the group that there was little justification for keeping the family's remaining shares, other than nostalgia and Jeanie keeping her controlling-ownership power for four additional years, according to multiple family sources. He circulated a proposal he hoped would satisfy all parties.

On the night of Aug. 10, two days before the sale, Lakers vice president of finance Joe McCormack called for a meeting of the Buss siblings to discuss a dissolution of the family trust and seek approval to lock down all family shares for four years under a new trust, according to ESPN's Dave McMenamin.

When the family discussed McCormack's proposal on Aug. 11, no mention was made of Walter's impending sale to Kushner and Iger. The family woke up to the news of the massive sale the following morning like everyone else.

On Aug. 17, ESPN's Shams Charania reported that Johnny, Jim, Janie, Joey and Jesse Buss had voted to sell the remaining family shares to Iger and Kushner, using "go-along" rights they had been given as part of the sale to Walter. (Technically, those rights can be only invoked once Walter officially notifies the family that he has signed a deal to sell, which hasn't happened yet.)

Jeanie was the only family member who did not vote to sell. In fact, she did not even respond to the vote that had been called a week earlier.

Later that day, her lawyer, Adam Streisand, sent a letter to the five siblings, challenging the legality of their vote based on a 2017 court order that required the two co-trustees, Janie and Joey, to always vote to ensure she remained the controlling owner of the team.

The siblings immediately responded to Streisand's initial letter with a statement of their own, reaffirming their desire to sell. They contended they needed only a majority (four of six votes and two of three co-trustees) to enact that go-along provision, according to sources with knowledge of the siblings' position.

Jeanie currently controls the Buss family trust, which owns 17.8% of the Lakers. NBA rules mandate that a controlling owner must own at least 15% of the team. An alternate governor must own at least 5%.

Still, multiple family sources said there have been settlement talks between the two sides over the past two months.

Each sibling stands to make an additional $371 million if the family sells the entirety of its shares via the go-along provision.

The siblings could also try to find a buyer at a higher valuation, a possibility fueled by a pitch, which The Wall Street Journal obtained, to Thrive Eternal investors in which the company projected the Lakers valuation to be at least $30 billion within a decade.

The dispute spilled back into the public on Oct. 7, when the five siblings formally filed a response to Jeanie's suit.

"Jimmy, Johnny, Janie, Joey and Jesse Buss, the five of six siblings who voted to sell the Trust's shares in the Lakers, today filed their formal opposition, demonstrating that Jeanie Buss's petition is legally and factually baseless," the siblings said in a statement issued to ESPN.

"While discussions among the siblings continue, their focus remains on facilitating the proposed transaction and the [Buss family] trust's participation in it, while ensuring that all beneficiaries, including Jeanie, are treated equally."

Nine days later, the five siblings submitted, on behalf of Joey and Janie, an additional filing, this one challenging Jeanie and her previous petition that seeks to remove them as co-trustees and void the siblings' 5-1 vote to sell the family's remaining stake in the team.

Through it all, the foundation of the dispute remains the same: whether the five siblings can sell their share of the team without Jeanie's approval.

A court date is set for Dec. 8 if no settlement is reached.

DONCIC WAS THE only person outside of the small circle of people close to Walter, Kushner and Iger who had any inkling how the sports world was about to dramatically change before Aug. 12.

The last time he had gotten a text from Seager, his longtime manager, at an odd hour was in February 2025, when she reached him after midnight and told him he had been traded to the Lakers.

This time, she had gotten a tip well after midnight at her home in Dallas that something big might be happening again. She texted Doncic, who was just waking up in Slovenia, alerting him to the possibility.

All summer, they had been planning a five-day team bonding retreat in Doncic's home country for his new Lakers teammates. On the first night, they'd all eat at his favorite restaurant, Cubo, in his hometown of Ljubljana.

Then, they'd play golf some 40 miles north on the perfectly manicured grounds of Royal Bled, sitting in a valley beneath the tree-lined peaks of the Alps. Another day was built around rowing lessons on Lake Bled, taught by Slovenian Olympian Jani Klemencic. Three high-speed boats, 15 Lakers, learning to row together.

Then, in one early-morning text, all those plans seemed secondary.

It was a stunning turn with no forewarning. Just a week earlier, Seager had met Jeanie and Rosen for dinner. Nothing had seemed amiss. At that point, Kushner had yet to engage Walter about the possibility of buying the Lakers.

Doncic had developed a good relationship with Walter and Jeanie Buss in the 18 months since he had come to Los Angeles, meeting and texting with both of them regularly. Walter even took him and a group of teammates to a Backstreet Boys concert at The Sphere in Las Vegas last summer, after Doncic agreed to a three-year, $165 million contract extension with the Lakers.

If the sale goes through and Kushner and Iger are approved by the NBA, and that is expected to happen by the end of the year or early next year, according to multiple sources close to the sale process, they'd be his fifth team owners across two franchises in the past three years.

By the time Seager called Doncic to tell him the deal was done, he had already processed the initial shock.

"There's not much that can shock me anymore," Doncic told her.

The next day, as he congratulated the new owners, he acknowledged the seismic move and posted on X:

"I've gotten used to big changes over these last few years."
